EntertainmentTab.title: Celebrity Traitors claim their first victim as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin
EntertainmentTab.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the second episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors.

As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player.

Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment.

"It's gutting to be the first out," Rajan said afterwards, noting that perhaps it was because he had been "a bit bullish with Richard" earlier in the day.

"But you know what, games are games, and just as there are winners, so there have to be losers."

The next morning, presenter Claudia Winkleman confirmed the University Challenge host's murder to the other players, joking: "That's what I call a starter for 10."

Acaster, meanwhile, reflected: "I'm gutted to not be a faithful anymore, I don't like lying. But if I don't join them, they'll kill me." You can't fault his logic.

The decision meant that Grant, an Oscar-nominated actor with a Razzie-worthy traitor strategy, did at least manage to commit one successful murder despite his shambolic first day.

The 69-year-old spent much of Friday's episode trying to repair the damage from his earlier exchange in the bar, where he blurted out that he was a traitor to Joe Lycett, Rob Beckett and several others.

Obviously a man who made such an excellent Spice Girls manager in the 1997 masterpiece Spice World: The Movie is hard for anyone to picture as a traitor, so many other players assumed Grant was attempting some elaborate double bluff.

Jama is off to a much stronger start. "I am quite shocked at my ability to just lie to everyone," the Love Island host said in the castle's diary room. "I'm an all-or-nothing kind of honey."

As the players gathered for breakfast, other theories began to surface. Mathematician Hannah Fry said she had spotted Leigh-Anne Pinnock putting on make-up late in the evening, perhaps heading to the turret.

"I think it's James," declared Jerry Hall, suddenly giving viewers hope that the new cast will be better traitor hunters than last year's. Until she clarified that she was talking about James Blunt, not Acaster.

As the players prepared to head out for the mission, conversations turned to far more important matters. "Do you have more teeth than a normal person?" Grant asked Rob Beckett.

The players made their way to the mission, which had the usual slightly convoluted rules that took Winkleman quite a while to explain.

In a nutshell, the celebrities were to be buried alive in pairs, with only one duo left above ground.

Ross Kemp was pre-selected by the traitors to be protected from burial along with his grave partner Romesh Ranganathan, who did a delightful dance when he found out he wouldn't be going underground.

Kemp and Ranganathan then had the opportunity to dig up some gold graves which would add to the prize pot, or alternatively dig up and free their fellow players.

They opted for the latter, which resulted in some other players struggling, external to get the soil off their faces. In the end, all the celebrities were released, with the exception of Fry and Hall.

The pair were freed early after Hall shouted the emergency word "Haggis!" – effectively a Scottish version of "I'm a celebrity get me out of here!" - because she was visibly uncomfortable being buried alive.

It might have led to an early release, but it ultimately guaranteed that either she or Fry will be murdered next, unless the traitors recruit again.

"Just you and me up for murder," Fry told Hall afterwards. "You'd better not be a traitor or I'm really screwed!"

In a flashback shown to viewers, Acaster explained the decision to protect Kemp from burial, telling his fellow traitors: "I think if we give it to Ross, he'll overthink it, and behave in a way that would draw suspicion."

Very clever. "You're a wonderful traitor," observed Grant. (Certainly better than him.)

Finally, it was time for the first banishment of the series, with Grant still in damage control mode.

"I have a slight pinprick of advantage," he told himself in the castle's diary room. "Nobody would possibly believe that anybody would be so stupid as to come forward and say 'I am a traitor'. I'm hoping that I do get away with it."

His fellow traitors clearly wanted to be supportive, but things were getting dicey.

Acaster described him as a "loose cannon", while Jama said: "I want to save him, even though he's dug himself the biggest hole imaginable."

Back in the castle, Ranganathan pointed out: "If somebody else had behaved like Richard, we wouldn't even be having a debate about this, you would just go 'you've got to vote for him'."

But others had a slightly different take. "Richard feels a little too easy," reflected actress Myha'la, "and then anybody pushing him feels suspicious to me."

Comedian Joanne McNally agreed some players were "using him as a fall guy and a decoy," although she did admit later that he's "made such a shambles of it now".

As discussions got going, it took a surprisingly long time for Grant's name to come up, as the other players debated other suspects such as Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The actress aroused suspicion because she was the first celebrity this year to receive a shield. The group seemed to have overlooked she only got that - in the opening minutes of the first show - after the other contestants voted her the most trustworthy.

But as discussion turned to Grant, Hesmondhalgh put forward one of the most convincing cases of the night.

"You came into the bar, and said you were a traitor," she told him. "It was a bold move. It was chaotic and we love you for your chaos.

"I think we are at risk of being the most idiotic group of faithfuls in the world, if we go for someone else tonight based on nothing at all, when somebody has come into the room and said 'I am a traitor'. There's no reason to say it unless you are."

Miranda Hart agreed that "the joy when he took off his blindfold" when Winkleman first selected the traitors made Grant look suspicious.

Viewers will have to wait until the next episode to see how the round table goes, as the episode finished before voting had even started.

(It's worth saying that, as cliffhangers go, this was far less irritating than ending an episode in the middle of a roundtable, as producers often do.)

"You've given us all a problem," Ranganathan told Grant as the episode drew to a close and the players prepared to vote. "By doing that, it was a big mistake by you, I feel like you forced our hand."

Admittedly, it's not looking good - the round table is shaping up to be a landslide vote against Grant. But we still wouldn't bet against him.

"I do not go down without a fight," he concluded. "I couldn't have survived showbusiness for four decades without a fight."

Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

EntertainmentTab.title: Spoilers: Is social media ruining gig surprises?
EntertainmentTab.text:
Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.

You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view.

When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.

But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.

Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.

Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months.

While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise.

Aurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul".

It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise".

The 20-year-old criminology student is a huge One Direction fan and says she just about managed to avoid spoilers for Styles' Together, Together tour over summer.

But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted".

"When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says.

"I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get."

Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them.

"I'm the type of person that loves to be prepared," the 22-year-old says.

"I love to know what the stage is looking like, what the set list consists of and where to stand."

McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing.

"Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds.

Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected.

Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run.

But the Guardian's deputy music editor Laura Snapes says it's not just fans who can benefit from these twists.

"One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."

Figures shared by TikTok with Newsbeat show posts using #CharliXCX have increased by more than 40% since the singer launched her Music, Fashion, Film tour last month.

If you want to avoid spoilers, there's only one thing you can do, according to Snapes: "You have to not look at TikTok.

"If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."

EntertainmentTab.title: Alison Hammond has heart check-up in hospital after rushing off This Morning while on air
EntertainmentTab.text:
Alison Hammond went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This Morning midway through Friday's show, but has assured followers she is "fine".

The presenter, 51, left the programme during its live broadcast, appearing to clutch her chest as she was assisted off the set by co-host Dermot O'Leary. He later told viewers she was "feeling a little unwell".

In a video posted from a hospital bed, external on Friday afternoon, Hammond said she had "a little bit of a palpitation" during the show but was feeling OK and was undergoing tests.

"I know you're all worried about me," she said. "Honestly, I am fine. First of all, I'm getting my old ticker checked out."

She continued: "I had a little bit of a palpitation, and now I'm getting it all checked out. But I think I'm OK. I'm hoping it was just a little panic attack or something like that."

The Birmingham-born presenter, who also co-hosts The Great British Bake Off, thanked This Morning's viewers for sending her "lovely messages" while apologising for her dramatic early exit.

"I'm so sorry I left you," she added. "I would never normally do that. I would never leave a TV show, so you know I wasn't very well.

"But hopefully I'm going to be all right. The doctors are so lovely, and they're checking me out, and hopefully everything's going to be fine.

"Everything is fine, look. I'm rocking it. Look how good I look," she joked, noting how she was still wearing her make-up from the show.

EntertainmentTab.title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
EntertainmentTab.text:
British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.

The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.

Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.

The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang.

In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.

He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.

The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.

To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.

In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.

The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.

I've Seen It is the closing track of Dean's breakthrough album, which was released in September 2025.

A sweet, acoustic ballad, it discusses the various types of love she's encountered in her life - from high school crushes to the love she has for her family and friends.

Speaking to W Magazine last year, she said the song was written after "I'd had a lot of red wine".

"When I heard it back for the first time, I burst into tears. It felt like the loveliest note to end on. Whether it's within your friends, your family, or just the love that exists in the strangers around you, it's there, and it's inside of you, too."

It is has been streamed on Spotify about 246 million times, while Just The Two of Us has racked up 948 million plays.

Withers' track was a collaboration with saxophonist Grover Washington, Jr and was originally released under the latter artist’s name.

It went to number two in the US charts in 1981 and earned Withers a Grammy for best R&B song. He died in 2020.

Dean picked up best new artist at this year's Grammys, while The Art of Loving reached number three in the US and number one in the UK, and was named album of the year at the Brit Awards.

EntertainmentTab.title: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards
EntertainmentTab.text:
One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards.

The move comes after the introduction of a controversial new category for Asian pop music, which critics fear will ghettoise genres like K-Pop and J-Pop.

BTS announced they would not submit songs for consideration in any category in July, saying they hoped their music "can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language".

Stray Kids, who recently scored their ninth US number one album, have now followed suit. In a short statement, their record label JYP simply said: "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys."

Stray Kids had previously refrained from giving a direct answer to questions about the awards.

During a press conference for their latest album, This and That, in August, singer Hwang Hyun-jin said: "We have never once set award results or records as our goal.

"Our top priority is for our fans to be happy and satisfied," he added.

The news will come as a blow to the Recording Academy, which organises the Grammys.

Stray Kids are phenomenally popular in the US, and recently headlined the Governor's Ball festival in New York, sharing the bill with Lorde and A$AP Rocky.

In the album chart, only one other band has scored more number one albums: The Beatles.

Earlier this year, all eight members of the band were given voting privileges at the awards, which gives additional weight to their decision to withdraw. BTS are also voting members of the Academy.

Stray Kids' announcement came hours after Grammys boss Harvey Mason Jr confirmed the new Asian pop category would go ahead at the 2027 ceremony.

"Over the past several weeks, the Academy has been conducting listening sessions and have been in dialogue with leaders of the Asian music community," he said in a statement.

"We heard candid feedback from people in our community who don't support the continuation of this category. We also heard from people who didn't have accurate information about the category, and having space to clear up misperceptions has been especially valuable.

"But by far, the loudest feedback we heard was from people who were enthusiastic supporters of the category, fellow music creators expressing their encouragement for keeping it."

He acknowledged that the decision "will not satisfy everyone" but said the Academy would continue to have discussions over the development of the award.

The Recording Academy announced the new category in June, saying it would recognise "artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets".

The prize had been under discussion for years. It was finally introduced after Golden, from the movie K-pop Demon Hunters, became the first K-Pop song ever to win a Grammy this February.

"As Asian pop's influence has continued to grow within our process, our members and trustees felt this was the right moment to create a category that more accurately reflects the genre's scale, artistry and global impact," organisers said at the time.

But the award received a decidedly mixed reception. Many felt it would stop Asian artists from receiving recognition in the main categories.

Others were upset by a stipulation that nominated songs should make "meaningful use" of an Asian language.

That requirement ruled out the two most recognisable Korean acts in America, BTS and Blackpink, whose latest releases are primarily sung in English.

The arguments against the Asian pop award are similar to those made by Latin artists about Grammy categories such as best música urbana.

While the intent is to recognise music of a certain geographic or linguistic origin, some musicians feel it ends up being exclusionary, with their music segregated from mainstream prizes like album or song of the year.

That perception was challenged this year, when Bad Bunny's Debí Tirar Más Fotos became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year. Rosalía's Lux is also expected to feature heavily in the nominations for next year's awards.

EntertainmentTab.title: First Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in under 30 minutes
EntertainmentTab.text:
The first batch of tickets for Glastonbury Festival have sold out in less than 30 minutes, according to the organisers.

The event will take place from 23-27 June 2027 at Worthy Farm in Pilton, Somerset, after a fallow year in 2026.

Coach tickets have now sold out after less than half an hour, after going on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday. General admission tickets go on sale at 09:00 BST on Sunday morning.

Jessi Dimmock from Glasto Cast, a podcast covering the festival, said: "It's the most stressful weekend of my year. I'll be there Sunday morning with my phone, my laptop, and my coffee and I will be stressed."

Festival organisers announced the first sell out in a post on Instagram.

General admission tickets are £408 for the 2027 festival. Dimmock said that she understands some people might "wince" at the higher prices.

"Anyone who has been to Glastonbury, it is magical. The small things are what makes it. It's just chaos in the best way," she added.

"I just think you can't count how much it is worth it for that money when you think of it in that respect.

"But I do understand, seeing it written down, you do wince at the fact that it now starts with a four rather than a three."

While the headliners for next year's festival have not yet been confirmed, Emily Eavis has said Oasis are not due to play despite speculation from fans.

The band announced a series of 2027 gigs across the UK, Ireland, Europe and the US last week, leaving a potentially Glastonbury-shaped hole in their calendar.

But Eavis put those rumours to bed in a direct response to one Glastonbury-goer on social media.

EntertainmentTab.title: Dolly Parton sings Jolene in Welsh in recording released after her death
EntertainmentTab.text:
A new version of Dolly Parton's Jolene is set to be released, with parts of the song sung in Welsh by the legendary country artist.

The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs.

The single will come out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.

In a teaser video released on social media, Star and Lewis explained how the song came to light.

As a proud Welsh speaker, Lewis, from Neath, had started translating some of her favourite tunes, and soon landed on the Parton classic, Jolene.

"Two years ago I posted a video of me singing the Dolly Parton classic Jolene in Welsh, external," said Lewis.

"I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada."

The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, which Lewis "jumped" at the chance to do, with Star then saying she would get her aunt involved too.

"Jada told me that her Aunt Dolly would like to sing with us on our version of Jolene. I think I fell to the ground," said Lewis.

"Definitely cried happy tears, and called my mother immediately."

BBC Radio Wales presenter Lewis said she had always loved Parton's music.

"To hear Dolly sing in another language, and in Welsh for the very first time, was unbelievable."

After understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation, Parton recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville, in early 2025.

Lewis had planned to go over to meet her to release the music, but Parton passed away before the meet-up could happen.

"It was devastating, not just for myself and our family, but for the entire world," Star said.

Lewis said the pair realised what a privilege it was to have recorded and collaborated "with one of the greatest musicians and women to grace this Earth".

"We did what she always told us to do. We got ourselves together and decided to finish what we started," Star added.

Star and Lewis said Parton was "proud" to sing in Welsh.

This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language.

She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011.

Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046.

In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd.

"Some of my mother's people, the Owens, are from there [Wales]," Parton later told Wales Online.

"I've been there about three times and it always feels good because it feels like family."

Star had also previously spoken about the family's Welsh connection.

She said the Owens side of the family, coming from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens, was believed to have come from Conwy.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales in 2024, Star said discovering that part of the family's history had been "really extraordinary".

Star suggested some of Parton's music, and her own, may have been inspired by her Welsh roots.

Parton's death brought renewed attention in Wales to the country music legend's Welsh links, with her heritage explored in a 2025 documentary.

Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, not Conwy as previously thought.

EntertainmentTab.title: Motörhead guitarist Phil Campbell died from multi-organ failure, inquest hears
EntertainmentTab.text:
Motörhead guitarist Phil Campbell died from multi-organ failure after suffering complications following "necessary" surgeries, an inquest has heard.

The Welsh rock star, who was the band's guitarist from 1984 until it disbanded in 2015, died aged 64 on 13 March.

Campbell's death could not have been prevented, St Pancras Coroner's Court heard on Friday.

The guitarist from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, underwent two liver transplants and bowel surgery at the Royal Free Hospital in London earlier this year.

The inquest heard he had previously drunk alcohol to excess but had been sober for seven years by the time of his death.

Campbell had suffered from Hepatitis C, external, but the inquest heard this had been treated.

While the second of the two liver transplants was successful, Campbell suffered further complications.

He underwent bowel surgery and was moved to intensive care, where he deteriorated rapidly.

He died in hospital on 13 March, with coroner Dr Richard Brittain recording his cause of death as multi-organ failure.

Brittain said: "My view is that there is nothing here to suggest his death could have been prevented."

He said Campbell died from "recognised complications of necessary surgical procedures".

EntertainmentTab.title: Oasis MTV Unplugged acoustic guitar sells for record £226,800
EntertainmentTab.text:
An acoustic guitar played by Noel Gallagher at Oasis's 1996 MTV Unplugged gig, and signed by him, has sold at auction for £226,800 setting a "world record".

Hertfordshire-based Propstore said it was the "highest price achieved at auction for an Oasis acoustic guitar".

It also sold a Yamaha C3 Grand Piano, for £81,900 which was used by Freddie Mercury to compose Crazy Little Thing Called Love. It was expected to sell for at least £200,000.

On the first day of its Music Live Auction on Thursday, the highest-selling lot was a notebook by the Queen frontman which contained handwritten working lyrics and notes from the Mr. Bad Guy recording sessions. It sold for £277,200.

Mark Hochman, the company's music specialist, said: "Setting a world record with Noel Gallagher's MTV Unplugged guitar is a fantastic result and a testament to the lasting connection fans have with Oasis.

"These results show how much collectors value pieces with a personal connection to the artists and their music."

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary
EntertainmentTab.text:
It is one of the prime minister’s all-time favourite films and has endured in the hearts of the British public since it was released in 1996. Ostensibly a story about a small town colliery band’s journey to the finals of Britain’s biggest brass band competition at the Royal Albert Hall, Brassed Off is unashamedly political.

“I think the people who went expecting a political film got the bonus of a bit of a comedy,” says its writer, Mark Herman, three decades on. “And the people who went expecting comedy got the bonus of the political message. I think anybody who went got a sort of bonus they might not have expected.

“On the face of it, a brass band film is not an easy pitch but word of mouth really rolled and suddenly it went on and on in places for months,” he recalls. “I thought it might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley for about two weeks,” laughs Herman. “So yeah, it’s amazing.”

Set in the fictional industrial South Yorkshire town of Grimley a decade after mineworkers brought themselves to destitution trying to save their livelihoods, it captures the hopelessness felt by former miners who struggled to keep themselves out of the dole queue during the slow and painful destruction of the mining industry by the Tory government.

Starring Pete Postlethwaite, Tara Fitzgerald and Ewan McGregor, it follows the Grimley Colliery Band as they await a judgment from British Coal as to whether their pit will be closed. A resounding success, Brassed Off went on to be number 85 in the BFI’s list of Top 100 British Films and spawned a popular stage play. To add to the plaudits, Andy Burnham recently named it as one of his four favourite films.

“How do I feel about that? It’s good!” says Herman. “It’s very flattering, but I’d have been more surprised if he’d have chosen Notting Hill.”

On its 30th anniversary, fiction and real life are set to collide when Grimethorpe Colliery Band – the group that inspired the film – heads to the real-life Royal Albert Hall to perform the music alongside a special screening.

The film’s success at the time was “surprising and very rewarding” but the enduring appeal, Herman believes, is because, “It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden.

“It’s really interesting hearing teens and 20-year-olds talking about the film, because it’s such an old film for them, but it really hits them. They get the message everybody got 30 years ago, because it’s still relevant and still plays.” But these films are a dying breed and Herman admits he is “fairly pessimistic” about the current state of the British film industry. “I feel like films like Brassed Off wouldn’t be made [now].”

“I’ve spent the last 10 years trying to get films similar to Brassed Off off the ground but can’t,” he says. “It seems to be blockbusters or micro-budget at the moment and there’s no space for mid-budget British films like those, films like I want to make.

“The studios are not as brave as they were,” he adds. “They’d stick their neck out, in what I call the old days. It was quite a risky film to make, Brassed Off, but now they seem to only want to put money behind dead certs.”

His favourite films of the last year were I Swear, the biography of a man with severe Tourette syndrome, and The Ballad of Wallis Island, an offbeat comedy drama written by and starring the comedians Tim Key and Tom Basden.

His path – from childhood in the East Yorkshire seaside town of Bridlington, to studying graphic design at Leeds Polytechnic (now Leeds Beckett University) and the National Film and Television School – would still open doors for youngsters in the industry, he thinks. But it is not an easy industry to break into, and now, in his early 70s, he thinks the advice he got when he was young – advice he took for a short while – to move to London, probably still stands.

“If I’d have [stayed in] London and networked I’d have probably done more films, but maybe not ones I care about as much,” he says.

Instead he wrote a powerful script, unashamed to spell out in no uncertain terms how the Conservative government destroyed communities and ruined lives, the effects of which continue. Higher mortality rates from suicide, alcohol and drugs developed – and persist to this day – in former pit towns and the shadow of Margaret Thatcher still lingers like an oil stain in these communities.

In a climactic scene in the Royal Albert Hall, Postlethwaite’s character, Danny, the band’s conductor, gives a memorable speech – later immortalised in the protest song Tubthumping by Chumbawamba – shouting: “I thought that music mattered. But does it bollocks. Not compared to how people matter.”

During filming, Birmingham town hall was substituted for the London venue, which was too expensive and “didn’t look anything like the Albert Hall”, Herman jokes.

Brassed Off Live will be a “strange experience … when our fake Albert Hall is on screen and you’re sitting in the Albert Hall. It’s a thrill. Thirty years ago would we ever imagine being in the Albert Hall still watching it? It’s amazing.”

EntertainmentTab.title: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy
EntertainmentTab.text:
Only when absolutely badgered will Lenny Rush admit that the title role of The Reluctant Vampire, Val, was written for him: “Shane Allen, the executive producer, loved the books when he was young, and he was the exec on Am I Being Unreasonable?. So yes, the scripts were written with me in mind. I’m so happy they were so good. I’d have felt awful if they said ‘We’ve written this for you’ and …” he trails off, pulling a face of exquisite pained courtesy.

Rush likens the show to The Naked Gun and Airplane!, and it has the writing team behind Alan Partridge, so can conjure awkwardness out of thin air. But it also taps into a comic tradition that goes even further back: a delight in the ridiculous, people talking to bats and gargoyles, invisible women interjecting by surprise, a surrealism whose comedy comes from the audacity of acting it with such commitment. “In my opinion,” says Rush, “sometimes things are labelled as a family show but they’re aimed at kids. I really do get the feeling that The Reluctant Vampire is for everyone.”

The Reluctant Vampire was written in the 80s by Eric Morecambe, in a surprising digression into children’s fiction from the comedy giant. It’s about the young scion of a bloodsucking household who doesn’t have any skills: his teeth aren’t pointy, he hates the taste of blood, and it transpires that he’s not a vampire at all but a rogue human. In the hands of Neil and Rob Gibbons, it’s like watching the essence of British comic sensibility – slapstick shot through with genuine pathos.

“You’ve got Tom Davis playing a vampire, this big character, with these big movements and this big voice, that can’t not attract a younger audience,” says Rush, “but the lines are genuinely funny.” The show opens with Davis in full vampire regalia, ready to strike an elderly victim in her bed, only for Rush to derail it all by rushing in saying he needs a wee.

Still only 17, Rush has been a fixture on TV for many years, starting aged seven in CBeebies documentary series Our Family. Then, aged eight in Apple Tree House on CBeebies he played Eli, a young rascal on an estate of well-intentioned young rascals. If you have children this age, you’ll feel like you’ve known him for ever, and if you are watching the latest season of Slow Horses, you’ll know him as the foul-mouthed, ancient-beyond-his-years kid whose steel trap of a mind effortlessly vanquishes the spies.

But his breakthrough role was in Am I Being Unreasonable?, for which he won a Bafta at 14 for best male performance in a comedy – and he was nominated again for the same award this year. That role, Ollie, along with his magisterial Bafta acceptance speech, sealed his reputation as a guy who has hacked your mainframe, and could effortlessly make you laugh at any time.

You can see in Rush’s performance as Val how much he’s gorged on Mr Bean, Alan Partridge, Monty Python. “I probably watched some things I shouldn’t have when I was younger,” he says. Never mind the age-appropriateness, how he found the time is anyone’s guess, since he has spent so long watching the British version of The Office that he knows it episode by episode, and has been working – as well as going to school – since he was seven. David Brent has always been his inspiration, and he delivers the kindest reading of that character I’ve ever heard. “You think: ‘What an idiot.’ Then you think: ‘What a not very nice man.’ Then you get to the end of series two, and there’s a really big element of pity. He’s just a man! Trying to find his way! He just wants to be part of the gang. It’s actually a tragedy.”

The opening episode of The Reluctant Vampire makes a lot of his stature, his parents measuring him and wondering if he’ll ever be tall enough to be a vampire. Rush, who has a form of dwarfism known as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, never went into acting for his condition to be a “talking point. I never thought I could be an inspiration for disabled people or young people.” The impact of his visibility on the world around him came as a complete surprise. “When Am I Being Unreasonable? came out, I started to get messages from mums, saying: ‘My little boy’s got a disability or a form of dwarfism, he’s struggling a bit at the moment at school. But he’s seeing you on telly and it’s giving him confidence.’ It’s so mad that I can be doing what I love and making people feel like that. I’m so pleased that that’s how people have seen it.”

Actually, though, the unvampiric vampire is a metaphor for belonging that is universal to teenagehood. “Going to school, trying to fit in, trying to impress, failing miserably. I think that’s why it’s so relatable. Even though it’s about vampires. Or you could see it as someone trying to find their place in society: ‘Am I doing this right? Am I good enough?’ It shouldn’t be so awkward, but it is.”

He’s not bringing a lot of his own experience of school to the travails of Val, incidentally – he never stopped attending, but was always off filming something and must have been artlessly cool. Which also made his parents very focused on his attendance. “My mum took school really seriously – not even necessarily, to be honest, the education side; she just found it very important for me to be seeing my mates. So I’d be on the PlayStation, and go: ‘I’m working with Gary Oldman,’ and they wouldn’t even look up from the game. You can get swept away really easily, on set. You have assistant directors coming into your dressing room, asking what you want for lunch, it’s quite insane. You have to have the right people around you.”

After Am I Being Unreasonable?, Rush got two episodes of Doctor Who, even if he wasn’t exactly a devotee. “I’ve not told Russell T Davies this, but I never watched Doctor Who. I knew what it was! I knew it was an honour to get asked. I knew it was a real moment in your career, especially to get cast young – I think Andrew Garfield was in it at a young age.” He played Morris Gibbons, a 13-year-old genius and adviser in the science unit, a really smart move after the role of Ollie, in which he’s also a genius but of a more cunning, domestic kind.

Am I Being Unreasonable? sometimes seemed to hang off his every expression – the plot of that show was absolutely wild, full of the worst parenting in the world, elaborately revealed secrets, dead pets. Rush’s command of the mood was what tethered it to earth. “Ollie was the breakthrough part, and after that I saw myself as an actor. But when I’d look online, before and after, people would say ‘He’s a great comic actor’ or ‘He’s a great young comic’. And I’m really thankful for that, but I never saw myself as a comedian or a comic actor. And as much as I love comedy, I don’t want that to stick as my thing.” His mum asked him recently whether he’d ever try standup. “It’s a bit of an annoying thing about British culture, and quite sad in my opinion, that it’s easy to get pigeonholed, and if I ever did try standup, it would take me further away from the Slow Horses kind of work.”

His next role is Dobby in the Harry Potter series that’s been beset by controversy – not just about whether actors can be in it without tacitly endorsing JK Rowling’s views, but also bizarre racist death threats to cast members. Rush hasn’t started yet, definitely hasn’t had any death threats, and is tight-lipped, saying only: “It’s pretty incredible – I feel so lucky, it’s insane.” It’s casting against type, this house elf, because Dobby’s not the effortless manipulator of all he surveys: his emotional top note is craven gratitude and anxious helpfulness. Maybe Val is a useful bridging role, because as a not-really-vampire, Rush ventures into new territories of panic and pitfall.

The Reluctant Vampire has palpable ensemble chemistry, between Rush, Sian Clifford as his mother, Davis as his dad, Asim Chaudhry as a Lurch-like character. Newcomer Gabriel Nagy is a great foil as his brother, a functioning, evil vampire. “I never felt like anyone was learning from me,” he says. “I felt like I was learning from them. I never felt like number one on the call sheet, having to keep everyone in high spirits. I remember Tom telling me, it sounds obvious but it was so true and so clever – if you’re doing a comedy, you want to make people laugh at home, so your goal in that scene is to make your co-star laugh. Try and get them to break.” They’re all pros, of course, so no sign of anyone corpsing; but like every classic comedy since TV began, you can feel that they’re smiling on the inside.

The Reluctant Vampire is on BBC One on Sunday 4 October at 6.40pm.

GeneralTab.title: Widdecombe suspect charged with planning acts of terror against Farage
GeneralTab.text:
The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Counter terror police said Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts.

The charge relates to activity which is alleged to have taken place between May 2024 and July 2026.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she knew the fresh charge would be "extremely concerning" and her "profound sympathies" were with Farage and his family.

"Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

"This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve."

The BBC contacted Reform UK for comment and a party source said: "This is exactly why Nigel needed £5m to protect his security for life."

Farage is currently facing a parliamentary standards watchdog probe into a £5m gift from a billionaire donor before he returned as an MP in 2024. The Reform leader has previously said the money was for his personal security.

Counter Terrorism Policing Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said the charge on Friday was the result of a "hugely intensive and complex investigation".

"This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge," she added.

Kerry, from Rotherham, is due to appear in court over the terror charge on Wednesday, police said.

Frank Ferguson of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division said prosecutors "worked closely" with police to bring the charge and would continue to work alongside them as the investigation continued.

Widdecombe was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing and would later become a Reform UK spokeswoman.

GeneralTab.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
GeneralTab.text:
The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.

President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".

Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."

It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.

European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.

GeneralTab.title: UK diesel prices top £2 a litre for first time, RAC says
GeneralTab.text:
The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group.

Diesel has now hit an average of 200.01p a litre, the RAC said, and petrol prices are also still rising, reaching 174.71p a litre on average.

The motoring group said price rises were "showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery onto motorists".

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide.

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refiners have further constrained supplies of diesel on the world market. China has also restricted exports of refined fuels.

Separately on Friday, G7 nations agreed at an urgent meeting to release 100 million barrels of oil to head off further price increases.

The G7 also agreed member countries would not impose export restrictions on each other, after US President Donald Trump threatened to ban shipments of American diesel overseas.

The move would have pushed up global prices of the fuel, but helped ease pressure on US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections.

RAC policy head Simon Williams said £2 was a "price threshold no one wanted to cross".

"This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders," he added.

UK businesses and consumers already feel like they are bearing the brunt of higher prices, with many saying it has made their lives increasingly difficult.

Even people who do not drive a diesel vehicle themselves face a knock-on effect from rising delivery costs or the higher cost of producing food.

Mark Means, who has farmed in Norfolk for over 50 years, said he was "frightened to death" by the rising costs of diesel.

He has spent £50,000 on new diesel tanks to try to ensure he has enough supply to harvest and plants crops, but the rising price is cutting into his margins.

"It feels like it's an assault," he said.

Steven Tompkins in Leicester said rising fuel prices mean driving instructors like him are having to increase their prices.

"When you've got kids who are working part time, they're on a tight budget and we're telling them that the prices are going to have to go up because of the fuel, it's hurting," he said.

GeneralTab.title: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections
GeneralTab.text:
The US jobs market saw a sharp slowdown in September, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in the final update before the midterm elections.

Headcounts were little changed in major sectors from tech to retail as hiring fell significantly from August, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September.

The figures signal a cooling US economy, which experts said reduced the likelihood of a series of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

The 29,000 jobs created in September was down from a figure of 133,000 in August, according to revised BLS figures for the month.

But George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, said while job gains have been a “rollercoaster“ this year, a single soft report is unlikely to point to a lasting collapse.

And Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said the lower figure was “not disastrous“, adding that a drop in government roles and temporary visa policy changes weighed on overall growth.

Jeffery Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, added that the data showed tension between “goods producing sectors that support the AI boom” and service industries feeling the effect of changes brought about by the tech.

“Given the overall softness of the labour market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is going lower,” he said.

The BLS report stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's insistence that America's economy is booming and it is the "hottest" nation in the world.

The disconnect is likely to present significant challenges as the president and his fellow Republicans hit the the campaign trail with just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections.

According to an AP/NORC poll released on Thursday, just 17% of Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Both are new lows for Trump, surpassing the lowest mark for Democrat Joe Biden during his presidential term.

There have been some indications that the president understands that his views of the American economy are out of step with those of most Americans.

"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing," he said at a White House event earlier this week.

articles.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.text:
The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.

President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".

Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."

It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.

European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.

articles.title: Two men charged with terrorism offences in Manchester
articles.text:
Two Iranian nationals who arrived in the UK by small boat have been charged with terror offences over an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester.

Rahman Salehi, 35, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool, are accused of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on or before 20 September.

The men were arrested in Manchester's Northern Quarter on the eve of Yom Kippur, considered the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said news that two Iranian men had been charged over the alleged plot would be "deeply distressing" to Manchester's Jewish community, as the city marks one year since the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.

Counter Terrorism Police (CTP) allege the two men were in contact with a third-party overseas, who may be in Iran, in relation to the plot.

According to CTP, the men are accused of obtaining instructions to make a chlorine bomb, acquiring liquids, components and equipment for such a device, researching potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.

It is understood the suspects arrived via small boat in 2020 and 2023. One was granted asylum, and the other has a live asylum claim.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors.

"Two suspects have been charged with planning a terrorist attack against Jewish communities in Manchester.

"This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

"I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue.

"The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further on this case. But I can say that we will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security."

articles.title: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
articles.text:
Riot police have clashed with protesters as thousands of students demonstrating over education standards disrupted more than 700 schools in France.

Fires have burned in the streets as high school pupils and others objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 1,747 people were arrested on Friday.

The protests began last week in the capital Paris and have spread across the country, with cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille affected.

French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said things had "gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance".

Darmanin said that 735 of France's 3,700 schools were now affected "one way or another" by the violent protests.

Announcing the arrests late on Friday, Nuñez told France's TF1 television network: "We are sliding into riot and urban violence, and we are using all intermediate means to put an end to it."

Meanwhile, Education Minister Édouard Geffray said the movement had been hijacked by non-students.

He told French broadcaster BFMTV that teachers had said "the people in front of me were not my students".

Earlier on Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.

BBC Verify has now authenticated two videos that show the man, who was later identified as an officer by a minister, being beaten up.

In the graphic footage, a group of young men are seen chasing him. The officer falls to the ground, and is subsequently punched and kicked multiple times in the head.

At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.

In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.

Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.

Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.

"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.

She said police actions had made things worse.

"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.

articles.title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
articles.text:
The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.

Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis.

Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off.

Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October.

That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

Energy UK said it accepted the government had already provided some support. VAT on electricity bills was cut on Thursday, and some levies were cancelled or shifted into taxation earlier this year.

But the trade body said these savings had been wiped out by high wholesale prices, paid by suppliers, that were the result in part of international events - namely conflict in the Middle East and the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

It said bills were soaring as they had in 2022 when they were driven up by the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

"We cannot afford to wait for the same scale of crisis before acting again. We must heed the lessons from that time," said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK.

She said that the urgent intervention needed was highlighted by growing levels of customer debt, the cost of which now added an average of £67 a year to everyone's bills.

articles.title: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places
articles.text:
The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to government.

The party said it would cost £2bn per year to build and run the new prisons, funded by spending cuts including to the foreign aid budget.

On Thursday hundreds of prisoners were released early, under new rules introduced to prevent jails reaching capacity, with around 4,500 due to be freed by next summer.

Labour blamed the previous Tory government for leaving "our criminal justice system at breaking point" and said the party's proposals were not "credible".

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday.

Prisons in England and Wales have been running close to capacity for years, with the latest government figures showing they are 98% full.

Under the latest early release scheme, eligible prisoners can now be released on a community licence after serving one-third of their jail sentence.

Those excluded include prisoners convicted of murder, manslaughter, a sexual or grooming-related offence, or a driving offence that led to a death.

The government has also effectively scrapped one-year jail terms.

The Tories said they would use extra prison capacity to reverse these measures.

An early release programme introduced by the previous Conservative government saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "A violent criminal doesn't become less dangerous just because the government has run out of prison cells."

She added: "[Labour's] answer is to let dangerous offenders out even earlier instead of building the prison spaces we need."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories are taking the public for fools. Across 14 years in government, they added just 500 prison places and closed 23 prisons.

"Now Kemi Badenoch expects the British people to believe they'll build 50,000."

Meanwhile, the Prison Governors' Association said "long-term investment" was needed and warned a "staffing crisis" would pose challenges to delivering new prisons.

If the party wins power, the Tories said they would introduce legislation early in the new Parliament to override planning and procurement barriers, allowing the process to be "fast-tracked".

It said the use of private finance would help speed up delivery and control costs.

There are currently around 89,000 useable prison places in England and Wales, according to the latest government figures.

The Tories said their proposals would increase this figure by more than 50%, with the vast majority of new places expected within the party's first Parliament in government - up to five years - and the full increase delivered within seven years.

The £2bn a year cost would be funded through savings in other areas, including cutting the aid budget by £1bn and reducing the budget of the Department for Culture Media and Sport by £1bn.

The Labour government has promised to add 14,000 extra prison space by 2031.

The Tories argued increasing prison places would cut crime and prevent reoffending by keeping serious criminals off the streets.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "Prison works. It works by punishing and deterring, but most importantly by incapacitating.

"Prison should keep violent and repeat offenders away from the law-abiding public."

articles.title: King's Caribbean tour will not shy away from 'darkest days of our past'
articles.text:
King Charles's upcoming Caribbean tour will not shy away from "the darkest days of our past", Buckingham Palace has said.

During the visits, the King is expected to face renewed calls to apologise for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade and be questioned on potential reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade.

The King and Queen Camilla are set to travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, with visits also to Bahamas and Guyana as part of the eight-day trip starting on October 27.

According to PA news agency, it is understood the government has not advised the King to apologise or offer reparations.

The King has previously expressed his "personal sorrow" at the UK's role in slavery.

A palace spokesperson said: "There are important discussions taking place in various fora about colonial legacy and the intergenerational impact of the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons.

"While these are primarily matters for Governments to address, His Majesty's previous statements on them have been unequivocal, describing them as an 'atrocity' which 'forever stains our history'."

The palace said the tour will "principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country".

Several African and Caribbean countries have called for a formal apology and reparations from countries that benefited from the transatlantic slave trade.

In September, Jamaica's government said it would raise a petition on the subject of slavery reparations with the King, the country's head of state.

Olivia Grange, the country's culture minister, said the petition would ask the King to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Last month, a Downing Street spokesperson said the transatlantic slave trade was "abhorrent" but the UK position was that it does not pay reparations.

articles.title: Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution, lawyer says
articles.text:
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator on Thursday night, after authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers say in court filings.

Pike, 50, was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.

Pike remained critically ill and was being treated at a Nashville-area hospital.

Lawyers for Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, are seeking to have her sentence commuted after the failed execution attempt.

Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution.

Hospital staff are working to save her life and clear the drug used, pentobarbital, from her system, the filing states.

During the execution attempt, prison officials tried to start intravenous (IV) lines by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers.

At one point, Pike herself offered guidance of where they could try.

"One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the filing states.

While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review into Pike's botched execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year.

The state's department of correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not not offered any explanations about what went wrong.

Pike's attorneys previously warned that her conditions, including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

In the latest filings, her lawyers allege that "at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body".

They are requesting that all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence is preserved.

Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said two doses of pentobarbital was enough that "she would have surely died" had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation.

The only possible explanation for her survival, Zivot said, "is that the pentobarbital blood level was never high enough to cause death" and that blisters on her arm after the botched execution indicated a ruptured vein.

So, instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, he said, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.

Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis may have also played a role, forming blood clots at the injection site that would potentially block pentobarbital from entering her veins.

Regarding the possibility the pentobarbital was degraded, Zivot explained that if this was the case, it could be due to factors including poor manufacturing or improper storage.

articles.title: Met Police urge pro-Palestine students to move 7 October protest
articles.text:
The Metropolitan Police is calling on the organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march planned to take place on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Israel to move the event.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said the force had been unable to identify the organisers behind the group, which calls itself the University of London Coalition.

He said that while the march did not meet the strict legal threshold at which police could request the home secretary to ban a protest, many Londoners would be marking "a day of mourning" with vigils to remember those who died.

The BBC has contacted the group for comment via social media accounts they appear to be associated with.

Harman said around 300 students were expected to march through central London, from King's College London in the Strand on Wednesday, finishing at University College London in Holborn.

He said they had demanded an end to what they described as a "genocide in Gaza".

"Serious concerns have been expressed about the impact of this march on students and staff, particularly those who are Jewish, the route, and the day it is being held," Harman said.

He urged anyone intending to join the protest to "reflect on the impact and distress it will cause on this very significant day, and exercise your right to protest on a different date".

Harman said the force had written to four London universities to ask them to engage with their students and staff and to take "all reasonable steps" to ensure students did not feel "excluded, targeted or unsafe" due to activity on their premises.

He said the letter acknowledged "the importance of freedom of expression, peaceful protest and academic debate" but also pointed to findings from the Community Security Trust over a rise in antisemitic incidents at UK universities since the attacks in 2023.

A march can only be banned if police consider it would result in serious public disorder, and that placing restrictions on it would not prevent that disorder from taking place. The decision needs approval from the home secretary.

Harman said he did not believe the strict legal threshold required in order to request such a ban had been met.

Neither the police or the home secretary can ban static demonstrations, although conditions can be placed on them.

Harman said that if the march went ahead, police would use their "full powers" to ensure there were "appropriate conditions" in place, including on the route and timing of the march.

Police say anyone who breaches conditions will be arrested and officers will take a zero-tolerance approach to hate crime.

Harman said although officers had made "every effort through formal and informal channels" to identify the organisers behind the event, they had been unable to do so.

"If it goes ahead, we will have to police it," he added.

Around 1,200 people were killed by Hamas fighters in the attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, and 251 people were taken hostage.

This triggered a massive Israeli military offensive in Gaza, which has killed over 70,000 Palestinians.

In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel is committing genocide, and a resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) in September came to the same conclusion.

More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.

Another pro-Palestinian protest is planned for Saturday 10 October, with 10,000 people expected to attend, as well as a counter-protest, which police said will be subject to strict conditions.

On Sunday 4 October, around 5,000 people are expected to attend a march in Whitechapel to mark the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street.

Police said they were not expecting disorder, but officers would be present in case of "disagreement between different groups" attending the event.

Harman said each of the events, along with the Holborn and St Pancras by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's seat on 8 October, represented a "challenge for policing".

He said officers had arrested three men, following reports of "intimidating and obstructive conduct" during canvassing in recent weekends, and "conflict between those canvassing and protesters".

Harman said that where police had intervened, it was for the purpose of preventing crime and disorder and not on any political preference, insisting "it's not a two-tier approach".

The Met says it expects more than 600 officers will be involved in policing the various protests and events over the next week, coming at a financial cost but also drawing officers away from day-to-day policing in London.
